title: A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge (BABOK Guide), International Institute of Business Analysis (IIBA)
text: The International Institute of Business Analysis defines business analysis as enabling change in the context of an enterprise by defining needs and recommending solutions that deliver value to stakeholders. Practitioners employ specialized tools and techniques to uncover opportunities and analyze requirements, driving value delivery and organizational success at strategic, tactical, and operational levels. The BABOK Guide is described as the standard for the practice of business analysis and is written for professionals who perform business analysis tasks. The guide organizes the practice into six knowledge areas that group related tasks by expertise domain, and it supports work ranging from small tactical initiatives to major business transformations. The Business Analysis Competency Model describes the knowledge, skills, abilities, and personal characteristics essential for effective business analysis professionals. Techniques represent the methods practitioners apply when performing business analysis tasks, with professionals selecting and applying techniques based on their experience, judgment, and demonstrated competencies to achieve successful outcomes. The framework also incorporates five perspectives addressing prominent business analysis disciplines, allowing professionals to apply the knowledge areas across different situations and organizational contexts. Together the knowledge areas, underlying competencies, techniques, and perspectives form a common framework of best practices intended to ensure consistency and quality in business analysis efforts across organizations and industries, and they form the basis for IIBA professional certifications.

title: BABOK: A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, SFIA (Skills Framework for the Information Age) reference
text: The BABOK Guide establishes business analysis as the standard for the practice of business analysis and addresses professionals who perform business analysis tasks. The framework organizes the discipline around six foundational knowledge areas that structure how analysts approach organizational change and improvement initiatives. The six knowledge areas are: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, Elicitation and Collaboration, Requirements Life Cycle Management, Strategy Analysis, Requirements Analysis and Design Definition, and Solution Evaluation. Planning and Monitoring encompasses selecting methodologies and establishing governance frameworks. Elicitation and Collaboration focuses on understanding stakeholder needs and presenting findings clearly. Requirements Life Cycle Management involves tracing, maintaining, and prioritizing requirements throughout their lifespan. Strategy Analysis examines current organizational states, defines desired futures, and assesses associated risks. Requirements Analysis and Design Definition specifies requirements through modeling and validates them against stakeholder needs. Solution Evaluation measures whether implemented solutions achieve business objectives and recommends improvements. The BABOK Guide emphasizes that practitioners need skills, deliverables, and techniques to achieve better business outcomes. The framework describes accountabilities and key activities rather than discrete tasks, recognizing that business analysis roles vary by organizational context and specialization. The content on this reference page was updated in 2023 to align with SFIA version 8 standards, with 2025 updates linking to SFIA version 9.

title: Software Requirements: Classifying Customer Input, Part 1, by Karl Wiegers (Jama Software, licensed content)
text: Karl Wiegers provides business analysts with a systematic approach to organizing customer feedback into distinct requirement categories. Rather than expecting customers to present information in tidy buckets, Wiegers acknowledges that requirements elicitation produces a more or less random array of information requiring careful classification and analysis. Business requirements address the fundamental question of project purpose. These statements articulate the financial or market value stakeholders expect to gain. Wiegers advises quantifying objectives, replacing vague targets like increase market share with measurable goals such as increase market share by X percent, which enables tracking progress and determining whether implemented solutions achieve intended outcomes. Use cases and user scenarios capture what people need to accomplish. Users often reveal these goals through workflow descriptions or statements beginning with I need to. User stories from agile methodologies follow a similar pattern, typically expressed as: As a role, I want to achieve some goal, so that I can reap some benefit. Business rules describe constraints governing specific actions under particular conditions. Wiegers offers this example: a chemist may order a chemical on the Level 1 hazard list only if his hazardous-chemical training is current, and advises listening for phrases like must comply with or if condition then something happens. Functional requirements document observable system behaviors and user capabilities. Wiegers emphasizes refining raw customer statements into precise specifications, cautioning that initial expressions may contain assumptions requiring clarification through dialogue.

title: Dimensional Modeling Techniques, Kimball Group (Ralph Kimball)
text: Ralph Kimball introduced dimensional modeling to the data warehouse industry in 1996, establishing foundational concepts that remain central to business intelligence design. The framework organizes data around two primary structures: fact tables containing numerical measurements and dimension tables providing descriptive context. The approach emphasizes star schemas and OLAP cubes as organizing structures that enable analytical querying. Core design principles include identifying the grain, the specific level of detail, for fact tables, and organizing dimensions hierarchically to support drilling down through data levels. Conformed dimensions serve as integration points across multiple fact tables, enabling users to drill across different business processes while maintaining consistent definitions. The enterprise data warehouse bus architecture uses an enterprise data warehouse bus matrix to map business processes against shared dimensions, facilitating coordinated development across organizational silos. Kimball techniques address how dimensions evolve over time through seven slowly changing dimension types, from Type 0, which retains original values, through Type 7, a dual Type 1 and Type 2 dimension. Advanced patterns include handling multivalued dimensions through bridge tables, managing hierarchical variations from fixed-depth to ragged structures, and specialized approaches for complex scenarios like heterogeneous products and real-time data. The methodology emphasizes starting with business requirements and data realities and conducting collaborative dimensional modeling workshops to align technical design with organizational needs.

title: How we structure our dbt projects, dbt Labs official documentation
text: dbt structure recommendations are grounded in a fundamental principle: establishing a cohesive arc moving data from source-conformed to business-conformed. Source-conformed data reflects the shape imposed by external systems beyond your control, while business-conformed data is shaped by your organization's unique needs, concepts, and definitions. dbt recommends organizing the models directory into three interconnected transformation layers. Staging models create atomic, modular building blocks from raw source data; prefixed stg_, they perform initial cleaning, renaming, and standardization, and follow the stg_[source_table] naming convention. Intermediate models stack purpose-built transformation steps with clear, specific objectives, preparing staging models to combine into the entities the business cares about, so complex logic is applied once in a dedicated location rather than repeated. Marts bring together modular pieces into wide, rich business-defined entities that serve end-users and analytics applications, using business entity names such as customers, orders, and products. Each model pairs a SQL file with accompanying YAML documentation. Key principles include consistency mattering more than perfection, so teams should explicitly decide on conventions, document them, and maintain them, with deliberate and communicated deviations acceptable. Layered modularity means stacking optimized transformation layers so each transformation happens in only one place, reducing duplication and improving maintainability. Disciplined structure creates a clear narrative not only in the data but also in the codebase and warehouse artifacts, which frees limited team bandwidth for solving unique and difficult problems rather than debating conventions.

title: Chart Guide, storytelling with data (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic)
text: The storytelling with data chart guide, authored by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, presents a resource for choosing and designing effective data visualizations. The guide catalogs more than 25 chart types with guidance on their appropriate applications. Recommended chart types include traditional options like bar charts, line graphs, and scatterplots, alongside specialized variants such as slope graphs, bullet graphs, and Sankey diagrams. The collection spans from simple formats such as data tables and dot plots to more complex multivariate displays such as bubble charts, treemaps, and spider charts. Additional options include waterfall charts for showing sequential changes, Gantt charts for project timelines, and choropleth maps for geographic data distribution. Knaflic's philosophy centers on eliminating ineffective visualization practices and guiding practitioners beyond basic software capabilities toward bespoke, custom charts and slides that an audience will love to look at. The guide's stated mission is helping rid the world of ineffective graphs, one 3D pie at a time, and it emphasizes that you do not need fancy tools to master data visualization and storytelling, just a bit of know-how and creativity. This chart guidance complements the broader storytelling with data lessons on understanding context, choosing an appropriate visual display, eliminating clutter, focusing attention where you want it, thinking like a designer, and telling a story, where clutter is defined as visual elements that take up space but do not increase understanding.

title: Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering, by Martin Zinkevich (Google for Developers)
text: This guide by Martin Zinkevich presents 43 rules organized across three phases of ML system development. The foundational philosophy emphasizes engineering discipline: do machine learning like the great engineer you are, not like the great machine learning expert you aren't. Most performance gains come from solid features and infrastructure rather than sophisticated algorithms. Pre-ML and Phase I principles prioritize fundamentals. Rule 1 advises against premature ML adoption, since simple heuristics often deliver half of the gains at lower cost. Rule 2 mandates designing metrics before building systems, enabling A/B testing and historical data collection. Rule 4 emphasizes keeping the first model simple while getting the infrastructure right: reliable data pipelines, clear success definitions, and serving mechanisms matter more than algorithmic sophistication. Phase II focuses on feature engineering and iteration. Rule 16 instructs teams to plan for continuous launches rather than one-time deployments. Rule 17 recommends starting with directly observed features before attempting learned representations. Rule 29 advises logging features at serving time for training reuse, Rule 33 recommends testing on forward-looking data after the training date, and Rule 37 emphasizes measuring training-serving skew. Rule 36 warns against positional features that create feedback loops where ranking position artificially inflates engagement. Phase III addresses plateauing gains: when simple metrics no longer suffice, teams must align ML objectives with broader product goals, explore qualitatively different data sources, and recognize that diversity and personalization often correlate less with popularity than expected, requiring explicit post-processing or objective modification.

title: Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance, scikit-learn official documentation (v1.9.0)
text: Overfitting occurs when a model is trained and tested on the same data, leading to artificially inflated performance metrics that do not generalize to unseen data. The standard practice to avoid this is holding out a test set, typically 20 to 40 percent of available data, for final evaluation. However, tuning hyperparameters on the held-out test set can leak knowledge into the model, again producing unreliable generalization estimates. Cross-validation solves this by partitioning training data into multiple folds without requiring a separate validation set. In k-fold cross-validation the training set is split into k smaller subsets; for each of k iterations a model is trained on k-1 folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, and the reported metric is the average across all k iterations. The scikit-learn default is cv=5. StratifiedKFold preserves class distribution within each fold, essential for imbalanced datasets. TimeSeriesSplit orders folds chronologically, training on earlier folds and testing on later ones to respect temporal dependencies. LeaveOneOut trains on n-1 samples and tests on a single sample, repeating n times, but is computationally expensive and high variance, so the documentation recommends 5 or 10-fold CV over LeaveOneOut. GroupKFold ensures samples from the same group never appear in both training and test folds. A critical principle is that data transformations such as scaling and feature selection must be fit on training data and applied to test data within each fold, which Pipelines automate correctly. Shuffling is off by default; enable it with shuffle=True and set random_state for reproducibility.

title: Classification: Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics, Google Machine Learning Crash Course
text: Accuracy measures the proportion of correct classifications overall, computed as (TP+TN) divided by (TP+TN+FP+FN). This metric works reasonably well for balanced datasets but becomes problematic with imbalanced data, where a model that constantly predicts the majority class could achieve high accuracy despite being ineffective. Recall, also called the true positive rate or TPR, captures the fraction of actual positives correctly identified, computed as TP divided by (TP+FN). It represents the probability of detection, answering what fraction of truly positive cases the model finds, and it is essential when false negatives are costly, such as in disease detection. Precision indicates the accuracy of positive predictions, computed as TP divided by (TP+FP). It represents the fraction of items flagged as positive that actually are positive, and it matters when false alarms carry significant costs. The false positive rate, or FPR, quantifies incorrect positive predictions among actual negatives, computed as FP divided by (FP+TN), and it becomes volatile with few actual negatives in the dataset. Precision and recall exhibit an inverse relationship, so improving one of them worsens the other; threshold adjustments typically decrease false positives while increasing false negatives, and vice versa. The F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balanced measure preferable for imbalanced datasets, especially when both metrics should be weighted equally. These metrics are all derived from the four cells of the confusion matrix: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

title: Lean Thinking and Practice, Lean Enterprise Institute
text: The Lean Enterprise Institute presents a framework developed by Womack and Jones in 1996 consisting of five sequential principles to guide lean transformation. Managers first specify value from the standpoint of the end customer by product family, then identify and eliminate non-value-adding steps in the value stream. They subsequently make the value-creating steps occur in tight sequence so the product will flow smoothly toward the customer, introduce pull mechanisms as flow develops, and continuously repeat the cycle to approach perfection with zero waste. The five principles are therefore value, value stream, flow, pull, and perfection. In a 2007 refinement, Womack and Jones condensed these concepts into three foundational elements: Purpose, Process, and People. Purpose requires correctly identifying customer value so the organization can cost-effectively solve problems and sustain profitability. Process focuses on optimizing the value stream across product development, fulfillment, and post-sale support, ensuring every step is valuable, capable, available, adequate, and flexible, with steps linked through flow, pull, and leveling mechanisms to maintain continuous operation. People represents the critical human element, assigning value-stream managers who engage teams and drive improvement through strategy deployment, frequent A3 analysis cycles, and standardized work practices. The overarching aim is to maximize customer value while minimizing waste, often referred to as muda, so that more value is created with fewer resources.

title: Value-Stream Mapping, Lean Enterprise Institute
text: Value stream mapping, often abbreviated VSM, is a foundational lean tool that visualizes the complete flow of materials and information required to deliver a product from order through delivery. The Lean Enterprise Institute describes it as diagramming every step involved in the material and information flows needed to bring a product from order to delivery. This whole-system perspective distinguishes VSM from narrower process-level analysis, enabling managers to optimize entire systems rather than isolated steps. The methodology operates in two phases. Teams first create a current-state map documenting actual material and information flows as they exist. They then develop a future-state map representing the target condition, that is, how flows should operate ideally. This iterative cycle helps organizations systematically identify and eliminate waste across their value streams. The institute notes that having a perfectly drawn current state map is not the point; the main intention of current state mapping is going through the process of trying to understand the dock-to-dock flow. VSM reveals waste sources that other analytical methods miss. By displaying both material movement and information signals together, the tool shows how upstream and downstream processes connect. This visibility enables managers to discuss flow decisions explicitly rather than allowing them to persist by default. The resulting maps become implementation blueprints, guiding how entire door-to-door operations should function, comparable to architectural plans before construction begins.

title: Kaizen, Lean Enterprise Institute
text: Kaizen, a Japanese term meaning continuous improvement, represents an organizational approach focused on making small, incremental enhancements to processes and systems. Rather than pursuing dramatic overhauls, kaizen achieves significant long-term benefits through sustained, company-wide participation. The kaizen methodology relies on PDCA, that is, Plan, Do, Check, Act cycles, where organizations identify improvement areas, develop implementation plans, execute changes, and evaluate results before iterating again. Critically, this approach requires establishing standardized work first. Taiichi Ohno, creator of the Toyota Production System, observed that there can be no kaizen without a standard. Stable operations, including functioning equipment, present workers, repeatable quality jobs, and available materials, must exist before meaningful improvement efforts, because without this foundation gains quickly disappear once teams stop focused improvement work. Organizations can pursue kaizen at different scales. Point kaizen addresses specific process improvements, while flow and system kaizen tackle broader operational integration. Kaizen events, described as intensive five-day improvement workshops, serve as capability-building activities. However, leaders should not rely solely on episodic events; steady daily kaizen, involving frontline workers and managers, develops sustainable problem-solving capability and prevents improvement gains from eroding. In this way kaizen functions as both a tool for doing and learning and a means of improving organizational culture over time.

title: The Five Forces, Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness, Harvard Business School (Michael E. Porter)
text: Michael Porter introduced the Five Forces framework in his 1979 Harvard Business Review article, establishing a foundational model for competitive analysis. The framework identifies five competitive pressures that shape industry dynamics and profitability. The five forces are: the Threat of New Entrants, the Bargaining Power of Suppliers, the Bargaining Power of Buyers, the Threat of Substitute Products or Services, and Rivalry Among Existing Competitors. Together these forces determine the competitive structure of an industry and its profitability. New entrants introduce capacity and pricing pressure; powerful suppliers extract higher prices and favorable terms; dominant buyers force down prices or demand additional services; substitutes redirect customer spending to alternative solutions; and intense rivalry erodes margins through price competition or escalating customer acquisition costs. Industry structure refers to the underlying competitive landscape shaped by these five forces, while industry profitability represents the returns available to competing firms. A critical insight is that industry structure changes over time and is not static. Technological innovation, regulatory shifts, and competitor actions continuously reshape competitive intensity and entry barriers. Porter's framework enables strategists to anticipate structural changes, identify advantageous positioning, and understand how profitability flows from both industry structure and a company's relative competitive position within that structure.

title: Creating a Successful Strategy, Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness, Harvard Business School (Michael E. Porter)
text: Porter defines competitive strategy as fundamentally about differentiation. Rather than competing on operational efficiency alone, successful companies deliberately choose a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value. The framework illustrates this principle through examples like Southwest Airlines and IKEA, which revolutionized their respective industries in the 1980s by establishing novel competitive positions. Porter identifies five core elements essential to a successful strategy. First, organizations must establish a unique value proposition that clearly distinguishes their offerings from competitors. Second, they need a distinctive value chain, deliberately choosing how operations will differ to support that proposition. Third, strategic trade-offs are crucial: companies must consciously decide what activities to avoid rather than attempting to serve all market segments equally. Fourth, successful strategies demonstrate fit across the value chain, where individual choices interconnect and reinforce one another across the organization. Finally, companies require continuity of strategic direction over time to realize competitive advantages. This framework contrasts strategy with mere operational effectiveness, emphasizing that sustained competitive advantage flows from strategic positioning rather than simply executing the same activities better than rivals. Because rivals can often imitate operational improvements quickly, it is the coherent system of trade-offs, fit, and continuity that makes a strategic position defensible over the long run.

title: What is Blue Ocean Strategy, by W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne (blueoceanstrategy.com)
text: Blue Ocean Strategy, developed by W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne, is defined as the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost to open up a new market space and create new demand. The framework distinguishes itself by making competition irrelevant rather than merely outperforming rivals, and its foundational insight is that market boundaries are not predetermined but can be reconstructed through strategic action. Red oceans describe existing industries with defined boundaries and accepted competitive rules; within this space companies compete for market share, products become commodities, and profitability diminishes as competition intensifies. Blue oceans represent unexplored market space where demand is created rather than contested. The framework positions these as distinct strategic orientations: red ocean strategy exploits existing demand within defined markets, while blue ocean strategy breaks the value-cost tradeoff by pursuing both differentiation and low cost simultaneously, an idea captured in the concept of value innovation. The framework is grounded in a decade-long empirical study spanning over 150 strategic moves across more than 30 industries. Rather than compete within existing industry structures, blue ocean strategy involves reconstructing industry boundaries. The methodology emphasizes building execution into strategy through visual, accessible tools and frameworks designed for organizational implementation, including step-by-step processes for assessing current market states, exploring pathways to new market space, and converting noncustomers into customers while managing risk.

title: Following the data: the research behind great managers, Google re:Work (Project Oxygen)
text: Google's foundational study, Project Oxygen, analyzed over 10,000 data points about its managers drawn from performance reviews, feedback surveys, and employee interviews. This multi-year investigation demonstrated that highly effective managers correlate with superior team outcomes, including improved happiness levels and reduced turnover. Project Oxygen identified ten essential behaviors distinguishing Google's most effective managers: being a good coach; empowering teams without micromanaging; creating an inclusive team environment; maintaining a productivity and results focus; communicating effectively and listening; supporting career development through performance discussions; having a clear vision and strategy; possessing relevant technical skills to advise the team; collaborating across organizational boundaries; and being a strong decision maker. Project Aristotle expanded this research by examining team dynamics across hundreds of Google teams globally. The study revealed that sales teams that worked together effectively brought in more revenue, exceeding their targets by an average of 17 percent, while less effective teams fell short of their targets by up to 19 percent, validating that how teams collaborate matters significantly more than individual composition. Google operationalized these findings through Google Manager Responsibilities, emphasizing three pillars: delivering results, developing people, and building community. Ongoing research confirms that employees with high-performing managers report enhanced productivity and a stronger sense of purpose.

title: Understand team effectiveness, Google re:Work (Project Aristotle)
text: Google's People Analytics team conducted Project Aristotle to identify what makes teams effective. The research, originally published in 2015 and informed by earlier Project Oxygen findings about manager effectiveness, studied 180 teams across engineering and sales divisions, combining qualitative assessments from executives, team leads, and team members with quantitative performance metrics. The research revealed a fundamental insight: what really mattered was less about who is on the team, and more about how the team worked together. Google identified five key dynamics of effective teams, ranked by importance. Psychological safety, where team members feel comfortable taking interpersonal risks without fear of embarrassment or punishment, emerged as the most critical factor. Dependability follows, reflecting reliable completion of quality work. Structure and clarity address the importance of clear job expectations and goals, often implemented through Objectives and Key Results. Meaning captures the personal sense of purpose individuals derive from their work. Finally, impact represents the subjective recognition that one's efforts contribute meaningfully to organizational goals. Notably, the research found that variables like team colocation, team size, individual performance metrics, and member seniority did not significantly correlate with team effectiveness at Google. This finding underscores that team composition matters less than team dynamics and interpersonal functioning, and it makes psychological safety a primary lever for HR and people leaders seeking to raise team performance.

title: SHRM Body of Applied Skills and Knowledge (SHRM BASK), Society for Human Resource Management
text: The SHRM Body of Applied Skills and Knowledge, or SHRM BASK, represents the evolution of SHRM's competency research, which began in 2011 when the organization studied thousands of HR professionals worldwide to identify critical success factors in the field. The framework emerged from this extensive research and was most recently updated in 2021, and it defines both the behavioral and technical dimensions essential for HR practice. The framework encompasses behavioral competencies including Leadership and Navigation, Ethical Practice, Relationship Management, Communication, Global and Cultural Effectiveness, Business Acumen, Consultation, and Critical Evaluation. These are complemented by one technical competency, HR Expertise, which covers the principles, practices, and functions of effective HR management. The competencies represent the types of behaviors that are integral for success in HR. The SHRM BASK serves dual purposes: describing the HR profession itself and defining the content areas for SHRM's certification examinations, specifically the SHRM-CP exam for operational roles and the SHRM-SCP exam for strategic positions. The framework also guides exam item development and the creation of study materials, with SHRM maintaining strict separation between its exam development and study resource operations to protect credibility. Organizations and individuals developing preparation materials reference this common framework to ensure alignment with professional standards across the HR field.
